extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders interested in international intellectual property systems
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes definitions, substantive eligibility standards, procedural features and cross‑border mechanisms for various forms of intellectual property (patents, trademarks, industrial designs, plant variety rights, geographical indications) and their international registration systems. Useful as a reference for understanding rights, requirements, and routes to obtain and maintain protection across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark definition and exclusive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another; the holder of a registered trademark has the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and can block unauthorized use of the trademark, or a confusingly similar mark, to prevent consumers from being misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarks can be registered for goods and services (service marks). Rights are territorial (limited to the jurisdiction of registration). Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided renewal fees are paid. Decisions to issue registrations via international routes remain with national or regional IP offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System – international trademark application and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Madrid System an applicant may submit a single international application in one language (English, French or Spanish) indicating the Madrid members where protection is sought and pay a single set of fees in Swiss francs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Madrid System simplifies filing and subsequent management (centralized recording of changes, central renewal). However, issuing a national registration remains the prerogative of each designated national or regional office; an international registration has the same effect as a direct national registration in a designated party only if that jurisdiction has not issued a refusal within a specified time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design subject matter and exclusive rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs refer to the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of a useful article (compositions of lines or colors or three‑dimensional forms) that give a special appearance to a product or handicraft; the holder of a registered industrial design has exclusive rights to prevent unauthorized copying or imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design protection is governed by national/regional laws; rights are territorial. In some countries industrial designs are protected via design patents rather than design registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design novelty/originality and term of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: An industrial design can be protected if it is new or original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once registered the term of protection is generally five years renewable for additional five‑year periods up to a total of 15 years in most cases; some jurisdictions differ (e.g., China provides 10 years from application date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System – international industrial design registration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System allows an applicant to register industrial designs in multiple territories by filing a single application with WIPO’s International Bureau and permits filing up to 100 different designs per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The System simplifies multinational registration and subsequent management (central recording of changes and single renewal procedure for designated territories), offering efficiency gains compared with direct national filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant breeder’s right eligibility criteria (UPOV)
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder’s right is granted only when a variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection, a plant breeder must file an individual application with every authority entrusted with granting breeders’ rights (rights are territorial). The UPOV Convention provides the framework for plant variety protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: US Plant Patent Act (PPA) scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PPA, whoever invents or discovers and asexually reproduces any distinct and new variety of plant may obtain a patent, excluding tuber‑propagated plants and plants found in an uncultivated state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to cultivated sports, mutants, hybrids and newly‑found seedlings; protection via patent under the PPA is distinct from breeder’s rights under UPOV/PVPA frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: US Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PVPA the United States protects all sexually‑reproduced plant varieties and tuber‑propagated plant varieties, excluding fungi and bacteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PVPA provides breeder’s‑type protection for sexually reproduced and tuber‑propagated varieties; the statutory scope differs from the PPA patent route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) definition and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical indication is a sign identifying a good as originating in a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that geographical origin; its main function is to indicate a connection between the quality, characteristics or reputation of the good and its territory of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs are commonly used for agricultural and food products but also apply to handicrafts and manufactured goods where characteristics derive from traditional skills or local resources. GIs may be geographical names or non‑geographical traditional denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use requirements for geographical indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications can only be used on goods that conform to the applicable requirements concerning the area of origin, processing method and typicity of the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goods produced outside the designated area or not meeting the specified requirements are prohibited from using the protected indication. Protection is territorial and to obtain protection abroad GI holders must seek protection under relevant national/regional laws or rely on international agreements where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellation of origin – stricter GI subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellation of origin designates a product as originating in a defined geographical area where the quality or characteristics of the product are due exclusively or essentially to that geographical environment, including natural and human factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellations of origin require a stronger link to territory than general GIs and thus form a more restrictive sub‑category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection mechanisms for GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs may be protected through sui generis systems (laws specifically designed for GIs), trademark law (notably collective and certification marks), unfair competition regulations, consumer protection laws, administrative and judicial decisions, or specific laws/decrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sui generis and trademark‑based protections often coexist; counting registered GIs is complicated because trademarks incorporating geographical terms are not always recorded separately. International registration systems (e.g., Lisbon, Madrid) and bilateral/regional agreements can facilitate protection abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System – international registration of appellations of origin/GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lisbon System provides a single registration procedure with WIPO that ensures protection in Lisbon contracting parties without the need for renewal, for as long as the appellation of origin/GI remains protected in its contracting party of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each contracting party retains prerogative to decide whether to protect a newly registered appellation/GI at national/regional level and may refuse protection on grounds foreseen in national law within one year of notification. The Geneva Act (2015) extended coverage to GIs generally and allowed accession by intergovernmental organizations and greater flexibility in recognizing national/regional means of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification marks vs collective marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification marks are usually awarded for compliance with defined standards and may be used by anyone able to certify that products meet those standards; collective marks distinguish goods/services of members of a specific group and are restricted to use by that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main difference in many countries is that collective marks are limited to members of an association while certification marks are available to any party meeting the owner's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification systems: Nice and Locarno
rubrics_metrics.description: Nice Classification: an international classification of goods and services for registering marks (45 classes: 34 goods, 11 services). Locarno Classification: an international classification for industrial designs (32 classes and subclasses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class counts (number of classes in a trademark application) and design counts (number of designs in a design application) vary across offices (multi‑class vs single‑class systems) and are useful for comparative statistics; under the Hague System up to 100 designs may be filed in a single application if they belong to the same class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance is an act by the applicant to keep an IP grant/registration valid (in force), primarily by paying the required fee to the IP office; the fee is sometimes called a maintenance fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademarks can be maintained indefinitely by paying renewal fees; patents, utility models and industrial designs have limited maximum terms and require periodic payments or renewals according to national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent definition and substantive patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is a set of exclusive rights granted for inventions that are new, non‑obvious (involve an inventive step) and industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are generally time‑limited (commonly 20 years). In return for exclusive rights, applicants must disclose their inventions in a manner enabling others skilled in the art to replicate them. Prior art comprises all public disclosures before a given date, which is relevant for assessing novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty – microorganism deposit for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves a microorganism and disclosure cannot be effected in writing, depositing a microorganism with any International Depositary Authority (IDA) under the Budapest Treaty is sufficient for patent procedure at national/regional patent offices of contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDA is a scientific institution (typically a culture collection) that stores microorganisms and furnishes samples; the treaty's mechanism eliminates the need to deposit samples in every country where protection is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT System – international patent filing procedure and phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT System facilitates acquisition of patent rights in many jurisdictions by centralizing the international phase (international search and possible preliminary examination) and then allowing entry into national phases where national/regional offices decide on patentability according to national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT reduces the need to file separate initial applications in each jurisdiction but does not substitute national/regional substantive examination or national decisions on grant; patent rights remain territorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application/grant counting for regional offices (statistical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and grants at regional offices are counted as equivalent to multiple national applications/grants, one in each member state; for certain regional offices (BOIP, EAPO, EUIPO, GCC, OAPI) each regional application/grant is multiplied by the number of member states for reporting by origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For EPO and ARIPO data, counting rules differ: each application/grant is counted as one application/grant abroad if the applicant does not reside in a member state, or as one resident and one abroad if the applicant resides in a member state. This equivalent concept is used for reporting statistics by origin.
